Check that the allocation matches the loss you could live through. The risk-profile stress test turns a stock share into a dollar loss. If a 30% fall in the equity portion would force you to sell, the allocation may be too aggressive, and changing it once is different from moving in and out.
Crash size. For two years in cash, a 45% crash needs about a 14% hit rate; a 35% crash about 21%. Larger falls reward correct warnings more.

Eligible Canadian dividends are grossed up: CRA’s instructions multiply the amount received by 138%, so CAD 100 becomes CAD 138 of taxable income. The federal dividend tax credit is 15.0198% of that grossed-up amount, about CAD 20.73, and Ontario’s 2025 worksheet applies 10% of the grossed-up amount, CAD 13.80. Net tax is about CAD 6.39.
Hold spending money outside the market. Cash needed within a few years belongs in savings or short-term deposits, not in equities you hope to time.
If you do act, write the rule first. State what will trigger a move, how much, and when you will return, then test it here with your own assumptions.
Interest is fully taxable: CAD 29.65 of tax on CAD 100.

Keep new contributions going. Contributing part of each paycheque continues through declines; FINRA describes dollar-cost averaging as a way to limit the effect of a significant decline on purchases, though regular investing cannot prevent losses on money already invested or guarantee a profit. Staging an existing lump sum is a separate decision, compared in the phased-investing guide.
Rebalance on a rule. A balanced fund or a written target mix sells some of what has risen and buys what has fallen; the rebalancing guide shows the drift during a crash.
Small crashes. With a 15% fall and a 25% rebound, staying out two years or more is “not reachable”: the rebound more than recovers the fall, so even a correct warning leaves the cash holder behind.

Time in cash. With a 25% crash, the required hit rate rises from about 10% for one year in cash to about 37% for two years, 56% for three and 74% for four. Each extra year out costs a year of ordinary growth on every false alarm, and after a correct warning it means missing the rebound.

A crash warning has to be right often enough to pay for the false alarms, and the required accuracy rises the longer you stay in cash and the faster markets rebound. Because nobody knows a signal’s future hit rate, a written allocation that you can hold through a fall usually serves crash fear better than switching in and out.
A fund passes its income through to you, and the label on that income sets the tax

A fund that is tax-efficient can still be a poor fit. A Canadian dividend fund concentrates in one country and often in a few sectors, such as banks, energy and utilities. A bond fund that pays fully taxable interest may be the part of a balanced portfolio that falls least in an equity crash. Diversification, risk tolerance, time horizon and fees usually matter more than the difference between tax rates on income types.

A fund’s income mix is not fixed. Bond funds pay mostly interest. Canadian equity funds often pay eligible dividends but may also distribute capital gains when the manager sells holdings. Index funds and ETFs with low turnover usually realize fewer gains, but can still distribute some. Fund Facts, annual reports and past tax slips show what a fund has paid; past distributions do not guarantee future ones, and a fund that changes its holdings can change its tax character.

A mutual fund or ETF held in a non-registered account is not taxed as one lump. CRA’s guidance on mutual funds explains that the interest, dividends and capital gains a fund distributes are reported by the investor in the year they are paid, even when they are reinvested in more units. Growth that stays inside the unit price is not taxed until the units are sold. The same 6% return can therefore produce very different tax bills depending on whether it arrives as interest, as Canadian dividends, as capital gains distributions or as a rising unit price.
A warning followed by a crash leaves the cash holder 12.1% ahead over that episode; a false alarm leaves them 6.5% behind. An unwarned crash affects both investors the same way.

Headlines about bubbles, recessions and “the next 2008” arrive every year. For someone with savings already invested, each one raises the same question: should I move to cash until it passes? A warning can turn out right, in which case cash avoids a loss. It can also be a false alarm, in which case the investor sits in cash while markets keep rising and then has to decide when to buy back. FINRA’s guidance on market timing warns that an investor who sells after a fall “very well might miss a subsequent recovery and rally.” A timing strategy therefore needs two decisions to go right: when to get out and when to get back in.

In a non-registered account, the form of a fund’s return matters as much as its size. Interest is taxed fully every year, eligible Canadian dividends receive a credit, realized gains are half included, and unrealized gains wait until a sale. A TFSA removes the difference. None of this makes a fund tax-exempt or its returns certain.

In the lowest brackets the dividend credits can exceed the tax on the grossed-up amount. With 14% federal and Ontario’s 5.05%, the model shows a negative dividend rate of about −8.24%: each CAD 100 of eligible dividends reduces tax on other income by about CAD 8.24. The credits are non-refundable, so that only works if there is other tax to reduce. The gross-up also raises net income, which can increase the OAS recovery tax or reduce income-tested benefits; the OAS recovery guide shows how that clawback is calculated. Use your own province’s Form 428 rates before drawing a conclusion.
Inside a TFSA, CRA says interest, dividends and capital gains are generally tax-free, including on withdrawal.

The correct warnings are generous: the cash period begins just before the crash year, so the investor avoids the whole fall. Real warnings are rarely so precise. An investor who moved to cash a year too early, or returned a year too late, would do worse than the model shows.

The dividend credit is designed to account for tax already paid by the corporation. It applies to dividends from taxable Canadian corporations; foreign dividends are taxed like interest and may have foreign tax withheld.

The ending values do not depend on the order of the episodes. Growth multiplies year by year, so the same set of years gives the same result in any sequence. The chart’s order is arranged only for display.

The episode chart shows why. Each correct warning left the cash holder about 12.1% ahead of the invested path over that two-year episode: two years of cash at 2.5% against a 25% fall followed by a 25% rebound. Each false alarm left them about 6.5% behind: two years of cash against two ordinary 6% years. Four small losses outweighed two larger gains. The unwarned crash hit both investors equally; no signal catches every fall.

The first chart shows the tax on CAD 100 of each kind of income at the default combined marginal rate of 29.65%: the 2026 federal rate of 20.5% on income from CAD 58,523 to CAD 117,045, plus Ontario’s 9.15% second-bracket rate, both from CRA’s 2026 rate table. These defaults are an example, not a recommendation of a province or a description of your bracket.

The heatmap repeats the 20-year comparison for pre-tax returns from 3% to 8%. At 3%, the interest fund keeps about 2.11% a year and the TFSA 3%. At 8%, the interest fund keeps about 5.63% and the TFSA 8%. The tax drag in percentage points grows with the return, because tax takes a share of every dollar of income.
The heatmap shows what drives the break-even rate:
The line crosses zero at about 37% of warnings being right. That share is a property of the signal, which is not known in advance and can change over time.

The model treats the hit rate as known. In practice it is the unknown that matters most. A signal that looked accurate in past data may have been fitted to those few episodes; markets and economies change; and crash warnings are often clustered, so an investor who acts on one may already be in cash when the next arrives. The OSC’s GetSmarterAboutMoney site cautions that trying to time the market often leads to losses when prices drop and opportunity costs when they rise, and that selling in a downturn locks in losses. Staying invested is not a promise of recovery by any date, and a long recovery can test even a patient investor.

The ranking changes with the tax bracket

The third chart reconciles each bar to the TFSA value. For the interest fund, about CAD 27,103 went to yearly tax and about CAD 18,946 is growth those tax payments would have earned had they stayed invested. The low-turnover fund pays no yearly tax and loses no compounding; its whole cost, about CAD 16,360, falls due at the sale. That is why deferral matters: the tax is not smaller in rate, but the money stays at work longer.

This guide holds the pre-tax return fixed and changes only its form. That separates two questions that are often blurred: how much a fund earns, which nobody knows in advance, and how the account and the type of income are taxed, which follows published rules. A fund is never tax-exempt on its own; the tax result belongs to the account and the investor.

This guide prices those two outcomes with one simple, editable model. It does not ask whether a crash will happen; it asks how accurate a warning would have to be for acting on it to beat staying invested.

Two right calls out of six did not pay for four false alarms

Under the defaults, a warning has to be right about 37% of the time just to tie with staying invested. With three correct warnings out of six, acting on them comes out about CAD 31,334 ahead; with one, about CAD 59,446 behind. The line chart shows how steep that trade-off is.

Use registered room where it fits. A TFSA removes the tax difference between income types; an RRSP defers tax but taxes withdrawals as ordinary income, so dividends and gains lose their lower rates there. The RRSP and TFSA timing guide compares the two.
